name: English II - Literature
description: A literature-focused Grade 10 course exploring world literary traditions — novels, short stories, poetry, and drama — with emphasis on close reading, literary criticism, cultural context, and analytical writing.

modules.title: Close Reading & Annotation
modules.objectives: Mark up a text actively by underlining key passages, circling unfamiliar words, and writing marginal notes; identify literary devices (imagery, irony, tone) on first encounter; formulate analytical questions that push beyond plot summary toward interpretation. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: University of Minnesota Open Education Network — Active and Mindful Engagement with Literature; focused, openly licensed guidance on annotation and close reading.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 1: Close Reading & Annotation (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: University of Virginia Library — Kate Chopin, The Story of an Hour; complete public-domain text transcribed and checked by UVA students and staff.
modules.assignment: Input: read the OEN active-reading guidance and the complete UVA text of Kate Chopin's 'The Story of an Hour.' Steps: (1) annotate the story with at least 12 substantive notes: three diction observations, three imagery or symbol observations, two shifts in tone, two patterns or repetitions, and two why/how questions; (2) for six notes, add a second sentence explaining a possible effect or meaning; (3) write a 250–300 word reflection that develops one interpretive claim from at least three annotations. Evidence and citations: quote only brief phrases from the UVA text and identify each quotation by the paragraph's opening words; cite both source titles in a short Works Consulted list, with no invented page numbers. Submit: one legible annotated PDF plus a 250–300 word reflection in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 35% complete, text-specific annotations; 30% reasoning from detail to interpretation; 20% accurate evidence and source labels; 15% clarity and presentation.

modules.title: The Short Story: Craft & Technique
modules.objectives: Distinguish narrative point of view and its effect on reader sympathy; identify situational, dramatic, and verbal irony; recognize the epiphany as a structural device; analyze how beginning a story in medias res creates immediate engagement.
modules.readingNote: Poe Museum — Edgar Allan Poe's complete public-domain text of The Tell-Tale Heart.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 2: The Short Story: Craft & Technique (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: Poe Museum — guided-reading edition of The Tell-Tale Heart with the full text and comprehension prompts.
modules.assignment: Input: read Poe's complete 'The Tell-Tale Heart' on the Poe Museum page; use the museum's guided-reading PDF only as a comprehension check. Steps: (1) make a four-row craft chart for point of view, opening structure, repetition, and irony; (2) enter one brief quotation and a two-sentence effect analysis in each row; (3) write a 500–600 word essay arguing how first-person narration and one other craft choice make the narrator less reliable while increasing suspense; (4) include one paragraph that considers a reasonable alternative reading. Evidence and citations: use at least four brief quotations from the Poe Museum text and identify them by the paragraph's opening words; include the Poe Museum text in Works Cited and do not cite unsupplied page numbers. Submit: one DOCX or PDF containing the chart and essay. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% accurate craft terms; 30% thesis and reasoning; 25% well-integrated textual evidence; 15% organization and conventions.

modules.title: World Poetry: Voice & Culture
modules.objectives: Analyze poems from African, Asian, Latin American, and European traditions; identify the speaker's voice and cultural identity within a poem; examine how historical and cultural context shapes poetic meaning; compare how poets from different traditions treat universal themes.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — Rabindranath Tagore's public-domain Gitanjali, translated by the poet; this module uses poem 35, beginning 'Where the mind is without fear.'
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 3: World Poetry: Voice & Culture (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: Project Gutenberg — direct section for Claude McKay's public-domain poem The Tropics in New York in Harlem Shadows.
modules.assignment: Input: read Tagore's 'Gitanjali 35' and McKay's 'The Tropics in New York' at the two named Project Gutenberg links. Steps: (1) annotate each poem for speaker, setting or implied situation, repeated ideas, imagery, and tone; (2) create a comparison table with at least four paired observations; (3) write a 600–700 word comparative analysis with a thesis explaining how cultural location shapes each speaker's idea of belonging or freedom; (4) distinguish the poem's speaker from the historical poet and state when a contextual claim comes from the source note rather than the poem. Evidence and citations: integrate at least two brief quotations from each poem, citing poem title and quoted phrase; list both URLs in Works Cited without inventing page numbers. Submit: the comparison table plus the essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% close reading of voice and imagery; 25% culturally careful comparison; 25% evidence-to-claim reasoning; 20% structure, citations, and prose control.

modules.title: The Novel: Setting & Atmosphere
modules.objectives: Explain how setting functions beyond mere backdrop to create mood and foreshadow events; analyze pathetic fallacy — the attribution of human emotions to nature or the environment; identify symbolic settings and explain their thematic significance.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — Mary Shelley's Frankenstein; complete public-domain novel. This module uses Chapters 5 and 10.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 4: The Novel: Setting & Atmosphere (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Writing Guide — textual-analysis planning, including how setting, imagery, diction, and context support an interpretive claim.
modules.assignment: Input: read Chapters 5 and 10 of Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein' in the linked Project Gutenberg text and review the OpenStax analysis planner. Steps: (1) make a two-column evidence chart for Victor's laboratory/bedroom in Chapter 5 and the Alpine setting in Chapter 10; (2) record at least three brief setting details from each chapter; (3) label where Shelley uses personification or pathetic fallacy and explain the projected emotion; (4) write a 550–650 word essay arguing how the contrast between enclosed and sublime settings develops Victor's psychological conflict and one broader theme. Evidence and citations: use at least four brief quotations, identifying each by chapter number; cite the Project Gutenberg text and OpenStax guide, with no fabricated pages. Submit: evidence chart plus essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% precise setting evidence; 30% analysis of mood and symbolism; 25% coherent comparison and thesis; 15% citations and writing quality.

modules.title: Character Psychology
modules.objectives: Analyze a character's motivation by examining backstory, desire, and fear; trace internal conflict through a character's thoughts, speech, and actions; identify foil characters and explain what they reveal by contrast; chart a character arc from beginning to end.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — Charles Dickens's complete public-domain novella A Christmas Carol. This module uses all five staves so the full sequence of Scrooge's memories, warnings, choices, and change is available.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 5: Character Psychology (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Writing Guide — textual-analysis questions for character motivation, conflict, development, and evidence.
modules.assignment: Input: read all five staves of Dickens's 'A Christmas Carol' at Project Gutenberg and the OpenStax textual-analysis guide. Steps: (1) build a beginning/middle/end character-arc chart for Scrooge; (2) identify his initial desire or fear, one internal conflict, and three causes of change drawn from at least three different staves; (3) compare Scrooge with Fred or Fezziwig as a foil using two specific contrasts; (4) write a 600–700 word character analysis that argues which one experience most changes Scrooge and why. Evidence and citations: integrate at least five brief quotations, labeled by stave, and cite both named sources; do not invent page numbers. Submit: an arc chart plus essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations or source labels. Evaluation: 30% evidence-based motivation and conflict; 25% causal account of the complete arc; 20% foil analysis; 15% quotation integration and citations; 10% clarity and conventions.

modules.title: Theme & Universal Questions
modules.objectives: Distinguish between topic and theme; identify multiple interlocking themes in a single text; explain how literature raises moral and philosophical questions without providing simple answers; write a theme statement that applies beyond the specific text.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — Anton Chekhov's The Bet in a public-domain English translation; the title story appears first.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 6: Theme & Universal Questions (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Writing Guide — critical-reading questions for moving from comprehension to supported interpretation.
modules.assignment: Input: read Chekhov's complete 'The Bet,' the first story in the linked Project Gutenberg volume, and review the OpenStax critical-reading questions. Steps: (1) list three topics raised by the story; (2) turn each topic into a complete, arguable theme statement; (3) attach two brief textual details to each theme and explain the connection; (4) choose the strongest theme and write a 500–600 word analysis of the moral question it raises about freedom, knowledge, money, or the value of life; (5) acknowledge one detail that complicates your interpretation. Evidence and citations: identify evidence by the story title and the paragraph's opening words, and cite both named sources without invented page numbers. Submit: theme-evidence matrix plus essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% defensible theme statements; 30% evidence-to-theme reasoning; 20% treatment of moral complexity; 10% source accuracy; 10% organization and style.

modules.title: Writing a Literary Analysis Essay
modules.objectives: Write a focused, arguable literary thesis; select and integrate textual evidence using the quote-sandwich method; write analysis that moves beyond plot summary to interpret meaning; maintain formal academic tone throughout a multi-paragraph essay.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide — complete planning, drafting, evidence, and revision process for textual analysis.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 7: Writing a Literary Analysis Essay (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL — MLA In-Text Citations: The Basics; use the rules for sources with and without page numbers.
modules.assignment: Input: choose one complete named text already supplied in Modules 2, 4, 5, or 6; reread that text and use the OpenStax analysis process plus Purdue's MLA citation guidance. Steps: (1) submit a one-sentence working thesis and a three-body-paragraph outline; (2) draft a 750–900 word essay with an introduction, three analytical body paragraphs, and a conclusion; (3) each body paragraph must use a quote sandwich with at least one brief quotation and explain how the wording supports the thesis; (4) revise once, marking three substantive changes in a short revision note; (5) include an MLA Works Cited entry for the exact online edition used. Submit: outline, final essay, and 100–150 word revision note in one DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% arguable, focused thesis; 30% analysis rather than plot summary; 20% evidence integration and accurate citations; 10% organization; 10% revision and editing.

modules.title: Greek Mythology & Classical Allusion
modules.objectives: Identify and summarize major Greek myths (Prometheus, Icarus, Narcissus, Orpheus, Medusa, the Trojan War); define allusion and explain how recognizing allusions deepens literary meaning; trace classical allusions in modern literature and popular culture.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — E. M. Berens, Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome; public-domain source for Prometheus, Narcissus, Orpheus, and Daedalus and Icarus.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 8: Greek Mythology & Classical Allusion (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: MIT Internet Classics Archive — Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book VIII; a public-domain classical version of Daedalus and Icarus for comparison with Berens.
modules.assignment: Input: use four passages in Berens's public-domain mythology text: the Prometheus passage under 'Theories as to the Origin of Man' beginning 'The theory of Hesiod'; the Echo and Narcissus passage under 'Nymphs' beginning 'There is a myth connected'; the Orpheus passage beginning 'The renowned singer Orpheus'; and the 'Daedalus and Icarus' passage beginning 'Daedalus, a descendant of Erechtheus.' Also use Ovid's Daedalus and Icarus episode in Book VIII at MIT. Steps: (1) create a four-row reference chart listing central figures, a three-sentence plot summary, a conflict, and two meanings available to later writers; (2) write two original 150–200 word micro-scenes, each using one myth as an allusion without naming it directly; (3) after each scene, add a 100-word commentary identifying the allusion and explaining how specific details carry the source myth's associations. Evidence and citations: identify each Berens passage by the locator and opening words above; cite Ovid by work and book when used; no page numbers are required. Submit: a chart, two micro-scenes, and two commentaries in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, direct source evidence, and accurate source labels. Evaluation: 30% myth accuracy; 25% purposeful allusive details; 25% explanation of transferred meaning; 10% source use; 10% clarity and originality.

modules.title: Drama: Greek Tragedy
modules.objectives: Define the characteristics of a tragic hero (hamartia, hubris, anagnorisis, peripeteia); explain catharsis and its function in Greek tragedy; read and analyze excerpts from Sophocles with attention to the chorus, dramatic irony, and fate vs. free will.
modules.readingNote: MIT Internet Classics Archive — Sophocles's Oedipus the King, translated by F. Storr; complete public-domain play.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 9: Drama: Greek Tragedy (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: MIT Internet Classics Archive — Aristotle's Poetics, Section 1; Part VI contains the definition and structural elements of tragedy used in this assignment.
modules.assignment: Input: read the complete MIT text of Sophocles's 'Oedipus the King' and Aristotle's definition of tragedy in Section 1, Part VI of 'Poetics.' Focus on the Teiresias confrontation, the Corinthian Messenger and shepherd revelations, and the final Chorus. Steps: (1) create an evidence table for hamartia/error, reversal, recognition, dramatic irony, and Chorus function; (2) enter one brief passage and a two-sentence analysis for each; (3) write a 600–700 word argument deciding how personal choices and prophecy interact in Oedipus's fall; (4) explain how one structural feature helps produce pity or fear, while noting that the precise meaning of catharsis is debated. Evidence and citations: cite play evidence by speaker and distinctive opening words, and Aristotle by work and section; do not invent line or page numbers. Submit: evidence table plus essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% accurate tragedy concepts; 30% nuanced causal argument; 25% textual evidence and analysis; 15% citations and prose.

modules.title: The Bildungsroman
modules.objectives: Define the bildungsroman as a coming-of-age genre and identify its structural conventions (naïve protagonist, initiation experience, loss of innocence, new identity); analyze how identity, belonging, and moral growth function in coming-of-age narratives; connect the genre to adolescent experience.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — James Joyce's Araby in Dubliners; direct link to the complete public-domain story.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 10: The Bildungsroman (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Writing Guide — questions for analyzing character change, structure, setting, and theme in fiction.
modules.assignment: Input: read Joyce's complete 'Araby' at the direct Project Gutenberg link and review the OpenStax fiction-analysis questions. Steps: (1) make a five-stage formation map: initial worldview, desire, obstacle, recognition, changed self-understanding; (2) attach one brief textual detail to each stage; (3) write a 550–650 word essay arguing whether the narrator's final recognition constitutes meaningful growth, painful disillusionment, or both; (4) connect the ending to a complete theme statement about adolescence without assuming that every coming-of-age story ends in maturity. Evidence and citations: use at least four brief quotations from 'Araby,' identified by the paragraph's opening words, and cite both named sources without page numbers. Submit: formation map plus essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% accurate tracing of development; 30% arguable interpretation of the ending; 25% evidence and reasoning; 15% citation, organization, and style.

modules.title: Postcolonial Literature
modules.objectives: Define postcolonial literature and its major concerns: colonial legacy, cultural identity, hybridity, representation, and resistance; analyze how José Rizal represents language, identity, institutions, and power under Spanish colonial rule in the Philippines; examine how literature by colonized peoples challenges dominant narratives without treating any culture as uniform.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — José Rizal's Noli Me Tangere in Charles Derbyshire's public-domain English translation, titled The Social Cancer; this module uses the Translator's Introduction and Chapters I–IV.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 11: Postcolonial Literature (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: Library of Congress research guide — concise, sourced context on José Rizal, Noli Me Tangere, and Spanish colonial rule in the Philippines.
modules.assignment: Input: read the Translator's Introduction and Chapters I–IV of Rizal's 'The Social Cancer' at Project Gutenberg, then read the Library of Congress José Rizal guide. Steps: (1) create a three-column chart for colonial institution or social rank, the narrator's or character's representation of it, and the power effect produced; include four rows; (2) write a 600–700 word analysis arguing how the opening chapters expose or complicate colonial hierarchy; (3) analyze at least one moment of code-switching, naming, honorifics, or translation and explain what it shows about cultural authority; (4) distinguish evidence from Rizal's novel, Derbyshire's introduction, and the Library of Congress context. Evidence and citations: use at least four brief quotations from the novel, labeled by chapter title, and cite the contextual source separately; do not invent page numbers or claim that one character represents all Filipinos. Submit: source-labeled chart plus essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% accurate use of postcolonial concepts; 30% close reading of power and representation; 20% source distinction and citations; 10% historical care; 10% clarity and organization.

modules.title: Literary Criticism Approaches
modules.objectives: Define and compare feminist, Marxist, and reader-response critical lenses; identify the kinds of evidence and assumptions each lens foregrounds; apply all three lenses to one story and explain how their distinct questions produce different, evidence-based interpretations and limitations.
modules.readingNote: University of Minnesota Open Education Network — Literary Theory and Schools of Criticism; use its overview of critical lenses together with the three explicit operational definitions supplied in this module assignment.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 12: Literary Criticism Approaches (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: University of Virginia Library — Kate Chopin's The Story of an Hour; stable public-domain text for applying multiple critical lenses.
modules.assignment: Input: read the OEN literary-theory overview, the complete UVA text of Chopin's 'The Story of an Hour,' and these course-supplied operational definitions: a feminist lens asks how gendered roles, voice, and power shape representation; a Marxist lens asks how class, labor, material resources, and ideology distribute power; a reader-response lens asks how textual cues interact with a reader's expectations and experience. Steps: (1) restate the central question of each lens in your own words; (2) produce a 180–220 word reading of the Chopin story through each lens, using at least one brief quotation and one explicit inference; (3) write a 150–200 word synthesis comparing what each lens reveals, what each leaves out, and which is most productive for this text. Evidence and citations: identify Chopin evidence by the paragraph's opening words and cite the OEN overview for the broader concept of critical lenses; treat the three definitions above as course material, and do not add unsupported author-biography or historical claims. Submit: three labeled analyses and one synthesis, 700–850 words total, in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and accurate citations or source labels. Evaluation: 30% accurate use of the supplied lens definitions; 30% distinct, text-grounded applications; 20% comparative synthesis and limitations; 10% citations; 10% clarity.

modules.title: Satire & Social Commentary
modules.objectives: Distinguish Horatian (gentle) from Juvenalian (harsh) satire; identify satirical techniques: irony, exaggeration (hyperbole), reversal, understatement, and parody; analyze how satire uses humor to expose and critique social flaws, institutions, or human behavior.
modules.readingNote: Project Gutenberg — Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal; complete public-domain text.
modules.videoNote: Genesis of Ideas International — English II - Literature, Module 13: Satire & Social Commentary (official GIIS lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: Oregon State University Guide to English Literary Terms — What Is Satire?, including Horatian and Juvenalian modes and A Modest Proposal.
modules.assignment: Input: read Swift's complete 'A Modest Proposal' at Project Gutenberg and Oregon State University's satire guide. Steps: (1) state the proposer's literal plan in 75–100 neutral words; (2) create a four-row evidence table for persona, verbal irony, hyperbole, and reversal or understatement; each row must include a brief quotation and its effect; (3) write a 550–650 word analysis identifying the real social targets, explaining why the calm economic persona intensifies the critique, and arguing whether the work is predominantly Juvenalian; (4) distinguish Swift from the fictional proposer. Evidence and citations: cite quotations by the paragraph's opening words and cite the Oregon State guide for genre definitions; use no invented page numbers. Submit: literal-summary paragraph, evidence table, and essay in DOCX or PDF. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: 30% distinction between author, persona, literal claim, and implied critique; 25% technique analysis; 25% evidence and reasoning; 10% source accuracy; 10% organization and style.

questions.question: Which annotation practice best moves a reader beyond passive reading toward active literary analysis?
options: Highlighting every sentence
Writing marginal notes that ask 'why' and 'how' questions about authorial choices
Looking up every unfamiliar word in a dictionary
Copying the passage into a notebook
questions.answer: Writing marginal notes that ask 'why' and 'how' questions about authorial choices
questions.explanation: Analytical annotation focuses on interpretation — asking why an author made specific choices — rather than merely recording comprehension. This pushes the reader into critical engagement with the text.

questions.question: A story that begins at a critical moment of action, with backstory revealed later through flashback or dialogue, is said to begin:
options: In chronological order
With an exposition
In medias res
With a frame narrative
questions.answer: In medias res
questions.explanation: In medias res (Latin: 'in the middle of things') is a narrative technique in which the story begins at a crucial point of action, creating immediate engagement. Backstory is provided afterward.

questions.question: In a short story, an epiphany is best described as:
options: The climax of physical conflict
The moment a character gains sudden insight or understanding
The exposition of the setting
The death of the antagonist
questions.answer: The moment a character gains sudden insight or understanding
questions.explanation: An epiphany (associated with James Joyce's short fiction) is a moment of sudden revelation or deep understanding that changes how a character sees themselves or the world.

questions.question: Which literary device appears in the line 'The city is a prison that holds us all'?
options: Metaphor
Simile
Alliteration
Understatement
questions.answer: Metaphor
questions.explanation: The sentence directly equates the city with a prison without using 'like' or 'as.' That implied comparison is a metaphor, and it suggests confinement rather than merely describing a physical building.

questions.question: Pathetic fallacy is a literary technique in which:
options: A character makes a logical error in reasoning
The weather or natural environment reflects or amplifies a character's emotions
The narrator speaks directly to the reader
Two characters have contrasting personalities
questions.answer: The weather or natural environment reflects or amplifies a character's emotions
questions.explanation: Pathetic fallacy projects human emotions onto nature or the environment — stormy weather during a tense scene, sunshine during a joyful one. It reinforces mood and atmosphere.

questions.question: A foil character is used in literature primarily to:
options: Replace the protagonist in the final act
Reveal traits of another character by contrast
Provide comic relief
Serve as the story's narrator
questions.answer: Reveal traits of another character by contrast
questions.explanation: A foil character has qualities that contrast sharply with another character (usually the protagonist), making the other character's traits more vivid and noticeable to the reader.

questions.question: Which of the following is a theme statement (not merely a topic)?
options: Courage
The story is about war.
War destroys the innocence of those who survive it.
The main character is a soldier.
questions.answer: War destroys the innocence of those who survive it.
questions.explanation: A theme is a complete statement expressing a universal idea. 'Courage' is a topic; 'The story is about war' is a plot description. A theme must make a claim about the human experience.

questions.question: In a literary analysis essay, the quote-sandwich method requires the writer to which of the following?
options: Introduce the quotation, include it, and then explain its meaning and significance
Use three quotations per paragraph
Place every quotation in its own paragraph
Let quotations replace the writer's analysis
questions.answer: Introduce the quotation, include it, and then explain its meaning and significance
questions.explanation: A quote sandwich frames textual evidence with context before the quote and analysis after it.

questions.question: Which Greek myth involves a craftsman's son who flew too close to the sun on wings made of wax and feathers?
options: Prometheus
Narcissus
Orpheus
Icarus
questions.answer: Icarus
questions.explanation: In Greek mythology, Daedalus made wings of wax and feathers for himself and his son Icarus. Despite warnings, Icarus flew too high; the sun melted his wings and he fell into the sea. The myth is often an allusion to hubris and the danger of overreach.

questions.question: In Greek tragedy, hubris refers to:
options: The moment of the tragic hero's self-discovery
The audience's emotional release at the end of the play
Excessive pride or arrogance that leads to the hero's downfall
The tragic flaw caused by a mistaken judgment
questions.answer: Excessive pride or arrogance that leads to the hero's downfall
questions.explanation: Hubris is extreme arrogance — the tragic hero's belief that they are above the laws of gods or fate. It is typically the catalyst that triggers the sequence of events leading to their destruction.

questions.question: The bildungsroman is a genre characterized by:
options: A detective solving a mystery
A hero's journey from naivety to maturity through formative experiences
A satire of political institutions
A tragic hero's rise and fall
questions.answer: A hero's journey from naivety to maturity through formative experiences
questions.explanation: The bildungsroman (German: 'novel of formation') follows a protagonist's psychological and moral development from youth to adulthood, typically through experiences that cause a loss of innocence.

questions.question: Which sentence is the strongest literary-analysis thesis?
options: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein was published in the nineteenth century.
Frankenstein is an interesting novel with many important events.
By contrasting Victor's enclosed laboratory with the open Alpine landscape, Shelley links secrecy to moral isolation.
This essay will discuss the settings in Frankenstein.
questions.answer: By contrasting Victor's enclosed laboratory with the open Alpine landscape, Shelley links secrecy to moral isolation.
questions.explanation: This sentence makes a debatable claim about how a specific craft choice creates meaning. The other choices provide a fact, a vague reaction, or a plan rather than an interpretation to prove.

questions.question: A writer from a society formerly ruled by Britain uses English but retains Indigenous words and speech patterns. Which postcolonial concern does this choice most directly explore?
options: Whether a colonial language can be reshaped to express and preserve a local identity
Whether every poem must use end rhyme
Whether a narrator must know every character's thoughts
Whether historical criticism should ignore language
questions.answer: Whether a colonial language can be reshaped to express and preserve a local identity
questions.explanation: The choice stages a tension between the history of English as a language of colonial power and the writer's ability to transform it through local vocabulary, rhythm, and perspective. It does not imply that all writers from formerly colonized societies make the same choice.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a topic and a theme in literature. Then write an original theme statement about the topic of 'power.'
questions.answer: A topic is a subject (e.g., 'power'); a theme is a complete statement expressing a universal idea about that subject (e.g., 'Unchecked power corrupts those who possess it and destroys those they rule'). The theme must make a claim applicable beyond any single text.
questions.explanation: Full-credit rubric (2 points): 1 point for accurately distinguishing a subject label from an arguable statement about that subject; 1 point for an original, complete power theme that is general enough to apply beyond one plot. A response that merely says 'power' or summarizes an event earns no theme-statement point.

questions.question: Define catharsis in the context of Greek tragedy and explain why Aristotle believed it was one of the most important effects of watching a tragedy.
questions.answer: In Aristotle's Poetics, tragedy arouses pity and fear and accomplishes the catharsis of such emotions. A strong response may explain catharsis as purgation, purification, or clarification, because the exact force of the Greek term remains debated; in each interpretation, the structured tragic action shapes the audience's response to suffering rather than producing emotion at random.
questions.explanation: Full-credit rubric (2 points): 1 point for connecting catharsis specifically to tragedy's arousal and working-through of pity and fear; 1 point for explaining why that audience effect matters to the form. Do not require the unsupported claim that Aristotle proved tragedy was medically therapeutic, and accept a well-explained purgation, purification, or clarification reading.

questions.question: Which annotation note is most analytically useful?
options: The repeated storm imagery suggests the speaker feels trapped and threatened.
This paragraph is long.
I read this page already.
The author uses words.
questions.answer: The repeated storm imagery suggests the speaker feels trapped and threatened.
questions.explanation: Useful annotation names a detail and explains a possible meaning or effect.

questions.question: Situational irony occurs when:
options: A character says the opposite of what they mean
The audience knows something a character does not
The outcome of a situation is the opposite of what was expected
The narrator directly addresses the audience
questions.answer: The outcome of a situation is the opposite of what was expected
questions.explanation: Situational irony is the gap between expectation and reality — when what happens is the reverse of what was anticipated. It differs from dramatic irony (audience vs. character knowledge) and verbal irony (saying the opposite of what is meant).

questions.question: In poetry, 'voice' most precisely refers to:
options: The volume at which the poem is read
The use of rhyme and meter
The distinct personality and perspective created for the poem's speaker
The number of stanzas in the poem
questions.answer: The distinct personality and perspective created for the poem's speaker
questions.explanation: Voice emerges through diction, tone, syntax, imagery, and point of view. Cultural identity may shape that voice, but readers should not automatically treat the speaker as identical to the historical poet.

questions.question: In a novel, a laboratory is repeatedly described as sealed, airless, and dim while its owner hides the consequences of his work. Which interpretation best treats the setting symbolically?
options: The room mirrors the owner's secrecy and moral isolation.
The room proves that scientific work can occur only at night.
The description supplies building instructions for a laboratory.
The setting has no function beyond locating the action.
questions.answer: The room mirrors the owner's secrecy and moral isolation.
questions.explanation: A symbolic reading connects recurring physical qualities of the setting to an abstract conflict. The sealed, airless space gives concrete form to secrecy and isolation; the other options either literalize the description or deny its pattern.

questions.question: Which evidence would best establish a character arc rather than a temporary change of mood?
options: The character makes a different kind of choice at the end after several experiences challenge an earlier belief.
The character smiles in one scene and frowns in the next.
The narrator describes the character's clothing in detail.
Another character enters halfway through the story.
questions.answer: The character makes a different kind of choice at the end after several experiences challenge an earlier belief.
questions.explanation: A character arc requires a traceable pattern of development: an earlier belief, pressures that test it, and later behavior showing a durable shift. A single emotion or descriptive detail does not establish an arc.

questions.question: Which of the following questions is most characteristic of a feminist critical reading?
options: How does the author's childhood affect the text's imagery?
How does the text portray gender roles and power dynamics between men and women?
What were the economic conditions of the period in which the text was written?
How does the reader's own background shape their interpretation?
questions.answer: How does the text portray gender roles and power dynamics between men and women?
questions.explanation: Feminist criticism examines how gender shapes representation, power, and identity in literature — asking whose voices are centered, how women are portrayed, and what assumptions about gender the text reinforces or challenges.

questions.question: In 'A Modest Proposal,' Swift's fictional proposer calmly presents selling infants as food as though it were rational economic policy. This strategy is best classified as:
options: Horatian satire — gentle mockery meant to entertain
Juvenalian satire — bitter, harsh attack meant to provoke outrage and reform
Parody — imitating Swift's own earlier work
Allegory — a story with a hidden moral meaning
questions.answer: Juvenalian satire — bitter, harsh attack meant to provoke outrage and reform
questions.explanation: The horrifying proposal, detached calculations, and polite persona create a dark attack on the treatment of poor Irish people as economic objects. The extremity is meant to expose indifference and exploitation, not to communicate Swift's literal position.

questions.question: Why is José Rizal's Noli Me Tangere useful for a postcolonial reading of Spanish-ruled Philippines?
options: Its Filipino author depicts colonial institutions and social hierarchies from perspectives those institutions marginalize.
It treats colonial rule as irrelevant background and avoids questions of power.
It was written by the Spanish colonial government as an official history.
It argues that one character can represent every Filipino experience.
questions.answer: Its Filipino author depicts colonial institutions and social hierarchies from perspectives those institutions marginalize.
questions.explanation: A postcolonial reading asks how empire organizes power, voice, identity, and representation. Rizal's novel makes those relations visible through Filipino characters and a critical portrayal of colonial institutions without reducing every character to a single national viewpoint.

questions.question: The tragic hero's hamartia is which of the following?
options: A tragic flaw, error, or mistaken judgment that contributes to the downfall
Their greatest strength
The final scene of the play
The comic relief character
questions.answer: A tragic flaw, error, or mistaken judgment that contributes to the downfall
questions.explanation: Hamartia is the flaw or error that helps bring about the tragic hero's reversal.

questions.question: Which statement moves from a topic to a defensible theme about knowledge in Chekhov's 'The Bet'?
options: Knowledge
The lawyer reads many books.
The story is about knowledge and money.
Knowledge pursued without human connection can transform values while also deepening isolation.
questions.answer: Knowledge pursued without human connection can transform values while also deepening isolation.
questions.explanation: The answer makes a general, arguable claim that can be tested against the lawyer's reading and isolation. The other choices name a topic, report a plot detail, or announce a subject without interpreting it.

questions.question: Reader-response criticism focuses primarily on:
options: The author's intentions when writing the text
The historical context in which the text was produced
The meaning a text produces through the interaction between text and individual reader
The economic class of the characters in the text
questions.answer: The meaning a text produces through the interaction between text and individual reader
questions.explanation: Reader-response theory argues that meaning is not fixed in the text alone but is created in the act of reading — shaped by the reader's own experiences, values, and cultural background.

questions.question: Which of the following allusions would most likely invoke themes of dangerous ambition and overreach?
options: A reference to Narcissus
A reference to Icarus
A reference to Orpheus
A reference to Pandora
questions.answer: A reference to Icarus
questions.explanation: The myth of Icarus, who ignored warnings and flew too close to the sun, is a classical allusion for dangerous pride and overambition. Narcissus alludes to self-obsession; Orpheus to love and loss; Pandora to curiosity and unintended consequences.

questions.question: Which action is most characteristic of the Chorus in a Greek tragedy?
options: Reflect on events, express communal concerns, and shape the audience's response.
Secretly cause every reversal while remaining unseen by the protagonist.
Replace the protagonist and resolve the conflict through combat.
Provide neutral stage directions without interpreting the action.
questions.answer: Reflect on events, express communal concerns, and shape the audience's response.
questions.explanation: The Chorus participates as a public voice within the drama: it reacts, advises, fears, and interprets. Its perspective can influence the audience without making it an all-knowing narrator or the agent of every plot turn.

questions.question: Which critical lens would most directly examine how economic class shapes a character's opportunities and limitations in a novel?
options: Biographical criticism
Feminist criticism
Marxist criticism
Reader-response criticism
questions.answer: Marxist criticism
questions.explanation: Marxist criticism analyzes literature through the lens of class struggle, economic power, and the relationship between dominant and marginalized groups — asking how capitalism, wealth, and class shape characters' lives and the text's ideology.

questions.question: What distinguishes a postcolonial literary concern from a historical one?
options: Postcolonial criticism ignores history entirely
Postcolonial criticism centers the voices and experiences of formerly colonized peoples, questioning whose history is told and from whose perspective
Historical criticism focuses only on the author's life; postcolonial criticism focuses on the plot
They are identical approaches
questions.answer: Postcolonial criticism centers the voices and experiences of formerly colonized peoples, questioning whose history is told and from whose perspective
questions.explanation: While historical criticism examines the time period in which a text was written, postcolonial criticism specifically interrogates the power dynamics of colonialism and asks how colonial and imperial histories shape identity, language, and narrative.

questions.question: Which technique is a defining feature of the bildungsroman genre?
options: The protagonist's death at the end
A narrator who is omniscient and removed from the action
A protagonist who undergoes moral, emotional, or psychological growth from youth to adulthood
A setting in ancient Greece or Rome
questions.answer: A protagonist who undergoes moral, emotional, or psychological growth from youth to adulthood
questions.explanation: The bildungsroman traces a young protagonist's formation — their development of identity, values, and worldview through formative experiences, often involving loss of innocence and hard-won self-knowledge.

questions.question: An allusion to Narcissus in a modern novel most likely suggests the character is which of the following?
options: Self-absorbed or dangerously fascinated with their own image
Overly ambitious and prone to hubris
A heroic warrior seeking glory
A messenger between gods and humans
questions.answer: Self-absorbed or dangerously fascinated with their own image
questions.explanation: Narcissus is associated with self-absorption and fixation on one's own reflection.

questions.question: When a literary analysis essay avoids plot summary and instead focuses on interpretation, it means the writer is:
options: Retelling the story event by event
Explaining what happens in each chapter
Arguing what events, images, or words mean and why the author made those choices
Listing characters and their traits
questions.answer: Arguing what events, images, or words mean and why the author made those choices
questions.explanation: Literary analysis moves beyond recounting what happens to interpreting significance — explaining how and why an author's choices create meaning, emotion, or thematic depth.

questions.question: Choose one of the three critical lenses studied in Module 12 (feminist, Marxist, or reader-response). Explain its core question and give one specific example of how you would apply it to a literary work from this course.
questions.answer: Responses will vary. Exemplar (feminist lens): The core question is, 'How does the text construct gendered power and whose voice has authority?' Applied to 'The Story of an Hour,' this lens examines how other characters interpret Louise Mallard's inner life for her while the narration briefly gives readers access to her private desire for self-direction. Brief references to the open window and the final medical judgment could support the claim.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for an accurate core question from one supplied lens; 1 point for a specific application that uses relevant textual evidence and acknowledges that the lens highlights some features while leaving others less visible.

questions.question: Explain the difference between Horatian and Juvenalian satire, and argue which type better describes 'A Modest Proposal' by Jonathan Swift. Support your answer with one specific detail from the text.
questions.answer: Horatian satire uses a comparatively tolerant, amused tone to expose folly; Juvenalian satire uses a harsher, indignant tone to attack vice or injustice. 'A Modest Proposal' is predominantly Juvenalian because its fictional proposer reduces impoverished Irish families to calculations and proposes selling infants as food to wealthy consumers. The grotesque plan and detached persona force readers to confront dehumanizing economic and colonial attitudes.
questions.explanation: Full-credit rubric (2 points): 1 point for a meaningful contrast in tone or purpose between Horatian and Juvenalian satire; 1 point for classifying Swift's essay with a specific textual detail and explaining how that detail supports the classification. Do not award the evidence point for merely repeating 'it is Juvenalian.'

quizQuestions.question: What is the primary goal of active annotation while reading a literary text?
options: To count how many pages you have read
To record plot events in order
To engage critically with the text by noting literary choices, patterns, and questions
To copy quotations for later memorization
quizQuestions.answer: To engage critically with the text by noting literary choices, patterns, and questions
quizQuestions.explanation: Active annotation is a form of dialogue with the text — recording observations about how and why an author writes as they do, not merely what happens.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is the most analytically useful margin note?
options: "Long paragraph"
"Repetition of 'dark' — reinforces the narrator's fear and isolation"
"Don't understand"
"Good sentence"
quizQuestions.answer: "Repetition of 'dark' — reinforces the narrator's fear and isolation"
quizQuestions.explanation: A useful annotation identifies a literary device, names it, and explains its effect on the reader or its contribution to theme. Vague observations add no analytical value.

quizQuestions.question: Which revision turns the margin note 'storm image' into an analytical annotation?
options: Storm image — look this up later.
Storm image — the repeated violence in the weather mirrors the speaker's rising fear.
Storm image — this sentence has eight words.
Storm image — I like this description.
quizQuestions.answer: Storm image — the repeated violence in the weather mirrors the speaker's rising fear.
quizQuestions.explanation: The revision identifies a pattern and proposes an effect on meaning. The other notes only flag, count, or react to the detail without interpreting it.

quizQuestions.question: Which narrative point of view gives the reader access to only one character's thoughts and feelings?
options: Second person
Third-person omniscient
Third-person limited
First person plural
quizQuestions.answer: Third-person limited
quizQuestions.explanation: Third-person limited narration uses 'he/she/they' but restricts the reader's knowledge to the inner life of one character. Third-person omniscient allows access to all characters' minds.

quizQuestions.question: In O. Henry's 'The Gift of the Magi,' each spouse sells a treasured possession to buy a gift for the other; as a result, both gifts are temporarily unusable. Which term best describes the gap between their loving intention and the unexpected result?
options: Verbal irony
Situational irony
Dramatic irony
Cosmic irony
quizQuestions.answer: Situational irony
quizQuestions.explanation: The reversal between the spouses' intended benefit and the gifts' unusable result is situational irony. The reader may know more than either spouse at moments, but the question asks specifically about outcome versus intention.

quizQuestions.question: In medias res as a narrative technique is best described as:
options: Ending the story at the climax
Beginning the story at a point of action, with backstory provided later
Telling the story in strictly chronological order
Using multiple narrators to tell the same events
quizQuestions.answer: Beginning the story at a point of action, with backstory provided later
quizQuestions.explanation: In medias res plunges the reader into an exciting or critical moment before the background is established. This technique creates immediate engagement and suspense.

quizQuestions.question: Why might an author choose third-person limited rather than third-person omniscient narration?
options: To keep readers close to one character's perceptions while withholding what others know
To reveal every character's private thoughts at the same time
To address the reader consistently as 'you'
To remove all uncertainty about characters' motives
quizQuestions.answer: To keep readers close to one character's perceptions while withholding what others know
quizQuestions.explanation: Third-person limited creates intimacy with one focal character and can build suspense or bias by restricting access to other minds. Omniscient narration, by contrast, can move among multiple characters' thoughts.

quizQuestions.question: When analyzing a world poem, 'cultural context' refers to:
options: The number of languages the poet speaks
The rhyme scheme of the poem
The historical, social, and cultural conditions that shaped the poem's creation and meaning
The length of the poem
quizQuestions.answer: The historical, social, and cultural conditions that shaped the poem's creation and meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: Cultural context encompasses the political history, social norms, traditions, and lived experiences of the culture from which the poem emerges — all of which shape its imagery, themes, and voice.

quizQuestions.question: In literary analysis, which statement best defines the speaker of a poem?
options: Always the poet themselves
The implied voice that narrates the poem, which may or may not be the author
The character being described in the poem
The reader of the poem
quizQuestions.answer: The implied voice that narrates the poem, which may or may not be the author
quizQuestions.explanation: The speaker is the voice constructed within the poem. Biographical evidence may support a connection to the poet, but first-person language alone does not prove that the speaker and author are identical.

quizQuestions.question: When comparing poems from different cultures, which claim avoids reducing either culture to a stereotype?
options: Both speakers use images of home differently; the contrast may reflect each poem's particular history and situation.
Every poet from the same nation speaks with one shared voice.
One unfamiliar image proves what an entire culture believes.
Cultural context determines a poem's meaning so completely that wording does not matter.
quizQuestions.answer: Both speakers use images of home differently; the contrast may reflect each poem's particular history and situation.
quizQuestions.explanation: The answer begins with observable textual evidence and frames context as a supported possibility. The distractors treat a poet as a spokesperson for everyone or ignore the text itself.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement best describes how setting functions in literary fiction?
options: Setting only tells the reader when and where the story takes place
Setting creates mood, influences character behavior, and can carry symbolic meaning
Setting is less important than dialogue in revealing character
Setting is only relevant in realistic fiction, not fantasy
quizQuestions.answer: Setting creates mood, influences character behavior, and can carry symbolic meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: In skilled literary fiction, setting is far more than backdrop. It establishes atmosphere, reflects character psychology, creates tension, and can embody the story's themes symbolically.

quizQuestions.question: Pathetic fallacy is the technique of:
options: A character making an emotional decision that leads to harm
Attributing human emotions or responses to nature or the environment
A narrator describing events with excessive sentimentality
Using weather to advance the plot rather than set mood
quizQuestions.answer: Attributing human emotions or responses to nature or the environment
quizQuestions.explanation: Pathetic fallacy (coined by John Ruskin) occurs when an author projects human feelings onto the natural world — 'the angry sea,' 'the weeping sky.' It reinforces emotional atmosphere.

quizQuestions.question: A symbolic setting is one that:
options: Describes a real historical location accurately
Changes multiple times throughout the narrative
Carries meaning beyond its literal description, embodying a theme or idea
Is described in exhaustive physical detail
quizQuestions.answer: Carries meaning beyond its literal description, embodying a theme or idea
quizQuestions.explanation: A symbolic setting has resonance beyond the literal — a prison symbolizes confinement of spirit, a garden symbolizes paradise or lost innocence, a locked room can symbolize repression.

quizQuestions.question: In Chapter 5 of 'Frankenstein,' Victor calls the night 'dreary' and the laboratory scene is marked by dim light, rain, and the Creature's unsettling physical features. What is the strongest interpretation of this setting?
options: It celebrates scientific work as orderly and reassuring
It creates a Gothic atmosphere that reflects Victor’s dread and the disturbing consequences of his project
It provides neutral weather details with no relation to mood
It proves the Creature is inherently evil before he acts
quizQuestions.answer: It creates a Gothic atmosphere that reflects Victor’s dread and the disturbing consequences of his project
quizQuestions.explanation: The darkness, rain, dim light, and Victor's horrified attention to the Creature's features create a Gothic atmosphere that externalizes his dread. The mood frames the consequences of Victor's project without proving a moral claim about the Creature.

quizQuestions.question: A character's motivation is best determined by examining:
options: How many pages of dialogue they have
Their physical description
Their goals, fears, and desires as revealed through actions, thoughts, and speech
The chapter in which they first appear
quizQuestions.answer: Their goals, fears, and desires as revealed through actions, thoughts, and speech
quizQuestions.explanation: Motivation is the 'why' behind a character's behavior. Readers infer motivation from what characters want, what they fear, the choices they make, and how they react under pressure.

quizQuestions.question: An internal conflict is a struggle that occurs:
options: Between the protagonist and the antagonist
Within a character's own mind — between competing desires, beliefs, or loyalties
Between a character and a natural disaster
Between two minor characters
quizQuestions.answer: Within a character's own mind — between competing desires, beliefs, or loyalties
quizQuestions.explanation: Internal conflict (person vs. self) is psychological — a character torn between two choices, wrestling with guilt or fear, or questioning their own values and identity.

quizQuestions.question: Which comparison most clearly uses a foil to reveal character?
options: Scrooge rejects companionship while Fred repeatedly welcomes others, making Scrooge's isolation more visible.
Scrooge appears in more scenes than Fred.
Fred and Scrooge are both characters in the same novella.
The narrator describes London before either character speaks.
quizQuestions.answer: Scrooge rejects companionship while Fred repeatedly welcomes others, making Scrooge's isolation more visible.
quizQuestions.explanation: A foil analysis names a meaningful contrast and explains what that contrast reveals. Mere co-presence, scene count, or setting description does not establish a foil relationship.

quizQuestions.question: Scrooge wants the security of keeping his wealth but is also drawn toward the belonging represented by Fred and Fezziwig. This tension is best classified as:
options: Internal conflict between competing values
External conflict with the weather
A conflict between two armies
A frame narrative
quizQuestions.answer: Internal conflict between competing values
quizQuestions.explanation: The struggle occurs within Scrooge as material security competes with connection and generosity. Fred and Fezziwig help expose that inner tension, but the central conflict is not a physical contest with them.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a theme statement (not a topic)?
options: Loyalty
The story is about family.
Family loyalty can both protect and imprison individuals who prioritize it above their own freedom.
There are many characters in the story.
quizQuestions.answer: Family loyalty can both protect and imprison individuals who prioritize it above their own freedom.
quizQuestions.explanation: A theme is a complete sentence expressing a universal insight. 'Loyalty' is a topic. 'The story is about family' is a plot description. The theme must make an arguable claim about the topic.

quizQuestions.question: When a text raises a moral question without resolving it, this suggests the author intends to:
options: Leave the reader confused
Indicate the story is unfinished
Engage the reader in active ethical reflection rather than providing easy answers
Show that the characters are morally weak
quizQuestions.answer: Engage the reader in active ethical reflection rather than providing easy answers
quizQuestions.explanation: Great literature often presents moral complexity without resolution, forcing readers to grapple with difficult questions themselves. This is one of literature's most important functions.

quizQuestions.question: In Chekhov's 'The Bet,' the lawyer sacrifices fifteen years of freedom while the banker risks two million rubles and later fears losing it. Which theme is most directly supported by their different stakes?
options: Pride can make people sacrifice freedom and security merely to prove themselves right.
Reading always makes a person reject society.
Wealth guarantees sound moral judgment.
Isolation affects every person in exactly the same way.
quizQuestions.answer: Pride can make people sacrifice freedom and security merely to prove themselves right.
quizQuestions.explanation: The wager grows from an argument neither man is willing to leave unresolved. The lawyer loses freedom and the banker endangers financial security, so their different costs support a theme about pride-driven sacrifice without claiming that their experiences are identical.

quizQuestions.question: Which evidence-and-reasoning pair best supports the theme 'Pride can distort moral judgment'?
options: The banker stakes a fortune during an argument; the rash wager turns disagreement into a destructive test of status.
The banker hosts a party; parties are important settings in fiction.
The lawyer reads books; reading is a major topic in the story.
Fifteen years pass; the story therefore has a long timeline.
quizQuestions.answer: The banker stakes a fortune during an argument; the rash wager turns disagreement into a destructive test of status.
quizQuestions.explanation: The first choice links a concrete action to the theme's claim about pride and judgment. The other choices identify facts or topics but do not explain how they support the stated theme.

quizQuestions.question: A literary thesis statement must be:
options: A question the essay will answer
A summary of the story's plot
An arguable interpretive claim that can be supported with textual evidence
A statement of fact that everyone agrees on
quizQuestions.answer: An arguable interpretive claim that can be supported with textual evidence
quizQuestions.explanation: A literary thesis takes a debatable interpretive position. 'The novel was written in 1900' is a fact, not a thesis. 'The novel critiques capitalism through its portrait of inherited wealth' is an arguable claim.

quizQuestions.question: In the quote-sandwich method, what comes immediately AFTER the quotation?
options: Another quotation
A plot summary of the chapter
Analysis explaining what the quotation means and how it supports the thesis
The author's biography
quizQuestions.answer: Analysis explaining what the quotation means and how it supports the thesis
quizQuestions.explanation: The quote-sandwich structure: introduction (context) → quotation → analysis (interpretation). Analysis is the most important part — it tells the reader what to take from the evidence.

quizQuestions.question: Which sentence provides literary analysis rather than plot summary?
options: The repeated door imagery turns each entrance into a test of the protagonist's willingness to change.
The protagonist opens the door and walks into the room.
Next, two characters discuss what happened earlier.
The final chapter describes the events that follow the argument.
quizQuestions.answer: The repeated door imagery turns each entrance into a test of the protagonist's willingness to change.
quizQuestions.explanation: Analysis explains the significance or function of a textual pattern. The other choices recount actions or sequence without interpreting why they matter.

quizQuestions.question: An allusion is a literary device in which an author:
options: Describes a setting in vivid detail
Makes an indirect reference to a person, event, myth, or other text
Compares two unlike things using 'like' or 'as'
Repeats a consonant sound at the beginning of words
quizQuestions.answer: Makes an indirect reference to a person, event, myth, or other text
quizQuestions.explanation: Allusion enriches meaning by borrowing the associations of the referenced source — a reference to Sisyphus suggests futile, endless labor; to Eden, lost innocence or paradise.

quizQuestions.question: In Greek mythology, Prometheus is primarily associated with:
options: Falling in love with his own reflection
Stealing fire from the gods to give to humanity and enduring a severe punishment for that defiance
Flying too close to the sun on wax wings
Opening a box that released all the world's evils
quizQuestions.answer: Stealing fire from the gods to give to humanity and enduring a severe punishment for that defiance
quizQuestions.explanation: In the assigned Berens account, Prometheus steals fire for humanity and is chained while an eagle repeatedly consumes his liver; Heracles later frees him. The myth therefore supports allusions to creative defiance, human advancement, punishment, and eventual release.

quizQuestions.question: A novel describes an entrepreneur whose profitable invention makes food and ordinary touch impossible as 'a modern-day Midas.' What does the allusion emphasize?
options: Artistic creativity without consequence
Wealth gained through a wish that also destroys ordinary human goods
Exile from home after losing a contest
Musical skill that persuades every listener
quizQuestions.answer: Wealth gained through a wish that also destroys ordinary human goods
quizQuestions.explanation: In the assigned Berens account, Midas gains the power to turn what he touches into gold, then discovers that even food is affected. The added context makes the allusion about gain becoming deprivation; it does not rely on the daughter episode found in some later retellings.

quizQuestions.question: A character ignores repeated warnings and pursues a risky achievement described as 'flying higher than anyone before.' What does an Icarus allusion add?
options: It frames the achievement as ambition shadowed by overreach and possible downfall.
It proves the character is literally the child of Daedalus.
It changes the story's setting to ancient Greece.
It guarantees that every reader will admire the character.
quizQuestions.answer: It frames the achievement as ambition shadowed by overreach and possible downfall.
quizQuestions.explanation: An allusion imports relevant associations from its source. Icarus adds a warning about ignoring limits; it does not make the modern situation literally identical to the myth.

quizQuestions.question: In Greek tragedy, hamartia most accurately refers to:
options: Their greatest achievement
An error, mistaken judgment, or 'missing of the mark' that helps produce the reversal
The climax of the play
The song sung by the Chorus
quizQuestions.answer: An error, mistaken judgment, or 'missing of the mark' that helps produce the reversal
quizQuestions.explanation: Hamartia can involve character, but it need not be a single permanent 'fatal flaw.' In Aristotle's account, the hero's consequential error helps move the action from prosperity toward suffering.

quizQuestions.question: Catharsis, as Aristotle defined it in relation to Greek tragedy, is:
options: The physical cleansing of the stage between acts
The audience's emotional purging of pity and fear through the experience of watching the tragedy
The hero's final victory over the antagonist
The chorus's final song
quizQuestions.answer: The audience's emotional purging of pity and fear through the experience of watching the tragedy
quizQuestions.explanation: Aristotle connects tragedy's arousal of pity and fear with catharsis. Because scholars debate whether the term means purgation, purification, or clarification, the secure point is that tragic form organizes the audience's encounter with those emotions.

quizQuestions.question: In 'Oedipus Rex,' the audience knows from the beginning that Oedipus has unknowingly killed his father and married his mother, while Oedipus does not. This is an example of:
options: Situational irony
Verbal irony
Dramatic irony
Cosmic irony
quizQuestions.answer: Dramatic irony
quizQuestions.explanation: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience possesses information that one or more characters do not. In 'Oedipus Rex,' the audience knows the terrible truth while Oedipus investigates the very crime he unknowingly committed.

quizQuestions.question: The defining structural feature of the bildungsroman is:
options: A story told in reverse chronological order
A young protagonist's psychological and moral development from naivety to maturity
A romantic plot between two adult characters
A detective investigating a series of crimes
quizQuestions.answer: A young protagonist's psychological and moral development from naivety to maturity
quizQuestions.explanation: The bildungsroman (novel of formation) traces a young person's growth through formative experiences — loss of innocence, moral tests, self-discovery — that transform them from naïve youth to mature adult.

quizQuestions.question: In the bildungsroman, the 'loss of innocence' typically refers to:
options: A character making a small mistake
A character discovering that the world is more complex, unjust, or painful than they had believed
A character forgetting their childhood
A character moving to a new city
quizQuestions.answer: A character discovering that the world is more complex, unjust, or painful than they had believed
quizQuestions.explanation: Loss of innocence in the bildungsroman is a pivotal moment — an experience that shatters the protagonist's naïve worldview and forces them to reckon with reality's complexity and moral ambiguity.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is the best example of a bildungsroman protagonist?
options: An all-knowing narrator who observes events from a distance
A mature adult who reflects on a decision made years ago
A young person who begins the story sheltered and naïve and emerges with hard-won self-knowledge
A villain whose motivation is revealed in a flashback
quizQuestions.answer: A young person who begins the story sheltered and naïve and emerges with hard-won self-knowledge
quizQuestions.explanation: The bildungsroman centers on a youthful protagonist's journey of formation — moving from innocence and ignorance through challenging experiences to a more complex, self-aware identity.

quizQuestions.question: Which ending most strongly supports reading a story as a compressed coming-of-age narrative?
options: After a failed quest, the young narrator recognizes that vanity shaped the earlier fantasy.
The narrator lists every object visible in a marketplace.
An adult character solves the conflict for the narrator without changing the narrator's view.
The story ends at the same emotional and moral position where it began.
quizQuestions.answer: After a failed quest, the young narrator recognizes that vanity shaped the earlier fantasy.
quizQuestions.explanation: A coming-of-age arc depends on changed self-understanding produced by experience. The recognition may be painful or incomplete; it need not prove that the character has reached full maturity.

quizQuestions.question: Postcolonial literary analysis most directly asks how a text represents:
options: Stories set during World War II
The experiences, identities, and cultural legacies of peoples who lived under colonial rule
Science fiction set in colonized planets
Ancient myths from colonial empires
quizQuestions.answer: The experiences, identities, and cultural legacies of peoples who lived under colonial rule
quizQuestions.explanation: The lens examines how colonial power and its legacies shape language, identity, institutions, and whose perspectives receive authority. It also avoids assuming that formerly colonized peoples share one uniform experience.

quizQuestions.question: In the opening chapters of Rizal's Noli Me Tangere, why is attention to titles, honorifics, and who controls conversation useful?
options: Those language choices reveal social rank and who is permitted authority under colonial hierarchy.
They prove every character has the same amount of power.
They matter only for pronunciation and never for interpretation.
They identify the novel as a Greek tragedy.
quizQuestions.answer: Those language choices reveal social rank and who is permitted authority under colonial hierarchy.
quizQuestions.explanation: Forms of address and control of dialogue are textual evidence of unequal status. A postcolonial reading asks how such everyday language makes institutional power visible.

quizQuestions.question: Which claim best demonstrates a postcolonial analysis of representation?
options: The narrator's shifting labels for local and colonial characters reveal whose viewpoint the social order treats as authoritative.
The novel contains many characters and several chapters.
The reader likes one character more than another.
The setting is decorative and has no relation to power.
quizQuestions.answer: The narrator's shifting labels for local and colonial characters reveal whose viewpoint the social order treats as authoritative.
quizQuestions.explanation: Representation concerns how language constructs people and grants or withholds authority. The answer links a textual choice to colonial power rather than merely naming content or reporting preference.

quizQuestions.question: Which practice is most responsible when making a claim about culture in Noli Me Tangere?
options: Tie the claim to specific narration or dialogue and avoid treating one character as representative of all Filipinos.
Assume every Filipino character expresses Rizal's personal beliefs.
Use the translator's introduction as if it were dialogue spoken by a character.
Treat all social differences in the novel as timeless national traits.
quizQuestions.answer: Tie the claim to specific narration or dialogue and avoid treating one character as representative of all Filipinos.
quizQuestions.explanation: Textual evidence supports a bounded interpretation; it does not authorize a generalization about an entire people. Keeping narrator, character, translator, and historical author distinct prevents overclaiming.

quizQuestions.question: Which question is most characteristic of a feminist critical reading?
options: How do gender expectations shape whose voice and choices carry authority in the text?
Which documented event in the author's childhood caused every image?
How many syllables appear in each sentence?
Which reader response is the only correct interpretation?
quizQuestions.answer: How do gender expectations shape whose voice and choices carry authority in the text?
quizQuestions.explanation: Feminist criticism examines how gender, representation, voice, and power operate in a text. It still requires close textual evidence and does not assume that one biographical event or one reader reaction fixes meaning.

quizQuestions.question: Marxist literary criticism examines a text by focusing on:
options: The author's religious beliefs
Class structure, economic power, and how wealth and labor shape characters' lives
The psychological development of the protagonist
The reader's personal history
quizQuestions.answer: Class structure, economic power, and how wealth and labor shape characters' lives
quizQuestions.explanation: Marxist criticism applies Karl Marx's ideas about class struggle and economic systems to literature, asking how class determines opportunity, how the wealthy exploit the poor, and what ideology the text promotes.

quizQuestions.question: Reader-response criticism holds that the meaning of a text:
options: Is fixed permanently by the author's intention
Can only be determined by expert scholars
Is created through the interaction between the text and each individual reader
Does not exist until a film adaptation is made
quizQuestions.answer: Is created through the interaction between the text and each individual reader
quizQuestions.explanation: Reader-response theory argues that a text has no single, fixed meaning — meaning is co-created in the reading act, shaped by each reader's experiences, values, and cultural background.

quizQuestions.question: Why can applying feminist, Marxist, and reader-response lenses to the same passage strengthen literary analysis?
options: Each lens foregrounds different questions, evidence, and assumptions that can be compared
Using three lenses guarantees one final interpretation
A lens removes the need to quote the text
The three approaches always produce identical conclusions
quizQuestions.answer: Each lens foregrounds different questions, evidence, and assumptions that can be compared
quizQuestions.explanation: Comparing lenses makes their selective focus visible: gendered power, class and material relations, or the reader-text interaction. The comparison can reveal blind spots, but every interpretation still needs textual evidence.

quizQuestions.question: Horatian satire is generally characterized as:
options: Bitter, angry, and morally outraged
Gentle, witty, and designed to amuse while gently mocking human folly
Focused on political assassination of specific figures
A form of parody that directly imitates another work
quizQuestions.answer: Gentle, witty, and designed to amuse while gently mocking human folly
quizQuestions.explanation: Horatian satire usually adopts a comparatively tolerant, amused voice toward folly. The label describes a dominant mode, not a rule that the work must be harmless or free of serious criticism.

quizQuestions.question: Juvenalian satire is distinguished from Horatian satire primarily by its:
options: Use of rhyming couplets
Tendency to praise rather than criticize
Bitter, harsh tone designed to provoke moral outrage and demand serious social change
Focus on romantic relationships
quizQuestions.answer: Bitter, harsh tone designed to provoke moral outrage and demand serious social change
quizQuestions.explanation: Juvenalian satire (named after Roman satirist Juvenal) is savage and morally indignant — targeting serious social injustices with the aim of shocking readers into demanding reform.

quizQuestions.question: Which observation best identifies Swift's fictional proposer as an instrument of satire?
options: His calm calculations treat people as commodities, exposing the cruelty of the reasoning he imitates.
He openly announces that every claim is a joke before making it.
He speaks in Swift's unfiltered personal voice and states the author's literal plan.
He avoids numerical language and economic vocabulary throughout the essay.
quizQuestions.answer: His calm calculations treat people as commodities, exposing the cruelty of the reasoning he imitates.
quizQuestions.explanation: The gap between the proposer's polite, quantitative voice and the inhuman proposal creates the satire. Recognizing that persona prevents readers from mistaking the literal plan for Swift's own position.
